title: The Phoenicians and the West: Politics, Colonies and Trade
author: Maria Eugenia Aubet
allowedUseNotes: Copyrighted scholarly monograph. Summaries in project's own words only; no reproduction of the book's text, maps, or figures.
summary: A standard synthesis of Phoenician trade, material culture, and expansion in the Iron Age. Aubet discusses Tyre's early alliance with the Israelite monarchy as a foundational episode in the book's own account of Phoenician commercial practice: Hiram of Tyre sending cedar logs, carpenters, and masons to build David a house (2 Samuel 5:11), with timber floated as rafts down the coast to a port (Joppa in the parallel Solomon narrative) and then moved overland to Jerusalem, later formalized under Solomon into an ongoing exchange of Phoenician timber and craftsmanship for Israelite agricultural produce (grain and oil). This project cites Aubet as comparative-ane corroboration that the text's own account of Tyrian cedar, carpenters, and masons matches known and independently attested Phoenician timber-export and craft-labor practice in this period -- coastal city-states with limited arable land and controlled access to Lebanese cedar forests routinely exported both raw timber and skilled labor to inland polities -- not as evidence for the specific historicity of this exact transaction, and not for any detail of construction (form, scale, plan) beyond what the text itself states.
